one_liner: C++20 xoshiro256++, ChaCha and Philox engines with xsimd SIMD bulk fill; beats std::mt19937_64 per call and in bulk.
what_it_does: simdrng provides Xoshiro256++, SplitMix64, ChaCha8/12/20 and Philox 2x/4x by 32/64 generators, each as a scalar class (XoshiroScalar), a runtime-dispatched SIMD class (XoshiroSIMD) and a compile-time best-arch class (XoshiroNative). Every engine is a UniformRandomBitGenerator with 64-bit result_type, so it plugs into std::uniform_int_distribution and friends, and adds uniform() for a [0,1) double, generate(buf, n) for u64 bulk fill and fill_uniform(buf, n) for doubles. Constructors take (seed, thread_id, cluster_id) to carve non-overlapping parallel streams. It also ships numpy.random.Generator-compatible Python bindings (nanobind), plus C, Fortran, MATLAB, Julia and JS binding options.
how_it_is_fast: The SIMD engines keep SIMD_WIDTH independent xoshiro256++ states in the lanes of four xsimd registers, lane i being the scalar generator after i jump() calls (2^128 steps), so one vector step yields 2/4/8 outputs on SSE2/AVX2/AVX-512. generate() writes whole 256-value blocks straight to the caller's buffer with unrolled unaligned vector stores; single-value calls drain a 256-entry cache refilled by the same code. The scalar uniform() uses the (x >> 11) * 2^-53 conversion from Vigna's notes instead of std::uniform_real_distribution, and the scalar engine is a constexpr inlined port of the reference xoshiro256plusplus.c. ChaCha and Philox gain more from SIMD because their per-value compute is heavier.
when_to_use: Filling large u64 buffers (Monte Carlo batches, tensors, NumPy arrays): XoshiroSIMD generate() measured 0.40 ns/value vs 0.94 ns for the scalar loop on an AVX2 EPYC 7763
Replacing std::mt19937_64 + std::uniform_real_distribution in a per-call loop: XoshiroScalar::uniform() was 1.32 ns vs 8.01 ns
Counter-based reproducible streams across threads or MPI ranks: Philox4x32 SIMD bulk fill was about 3.5x its scalar version, and Philox derives sub-streams from (seed, counter) without coordination
One binary shipped to mixed x86 fleets, built with SIMDRNG_DISPATCH=ON so the AVX-512/AVX2/SSE2 tier is picked at runtime (NEON and RVV128 on other ISAs)
Python code that wants a drop-in numpy.random.Generator backed by a GIL-released C++ bulk fill
when_not_to_use: Cheap engines consumed one value at a time: XoshiroSIMD/XoshiroNative cost 2.81-2.82 ns per call vs 0.94 ns for XoshiroScalar because of the buffered read, so stay scalar there

Results that must be bit-identical across machines: the SIMD stream interleaves SIMD_WIDTH lanes, so the same seed gives different sequences on SSE2 (2 lanes), AVX2 (4) and AVX-512 (8); use XoshiroScalar or Philox/ChaCha with fixed counters
Double-precision bulk fill expecting the u64 speedup: fill_uniform went through a 256-value temporary and measured 4219 ns vs 5116 ns scalar per 4096 doubles (about 1.2x, derived from page data)
Projects that need a stable API or a permissive OSI license: pre-1.0 with no tagged release, and the BSD-3-Clause-Attribution license adds an acknowledgement clause for every redistribution

Security uses, unless you vet it yourself: the ChaCha guide calls ChaCha12/20 'the cryptographic choices', but there is no claim of constant-time code, key handling or reseeding, so treat it as a statistical generator

integration.form: header-only for scalar and *Native types; static/shared lib (small dispatch TUs) for the runtime-dispatched *SIMD types; single-header amalgamation on the single-header branch (Native types only)
integration.dependencies: none for the scalar path; xsimd 14.3.0 and DiamonDinoia/poet (pinned SHA) for SIMD types, fetched via CPM; Google Benchmark/Catch2 for tests; nanobind for Python
integration.min_toolchain: C++20 (INTERFACE cxx_std_20), CMake 3.29; CI covers GCC 13/14, Clang 18/20, Apple Clang (macos-14) and MSVC (windows-2022)
integration.platforms: x86-64 (SSE2/AVX2/AVX-512BW tiers), aarch64 (NEON dispatch tier; an SVE instantiation is declared when xsimd has SVE enabled), riscv64 (RVV, VLEN 128); scalar path anywhere
integration.thread_safety: Instances hold no shared or global state and are heap-free (docs/benchmarks.rst), so one generator per thread is safe; a single instance is not synchronized
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: satisfies UniformRandomBitGenerator and works with std distributions, but it is a different generator from std::mt19937_64 (different sequence), and the speedup on doubles needs uniform()/fill_uniform rather than std::uniform_real_distribution

gotchas: simdrng::Xoshiro is not the scalar engine: xoshiro.hpp aliases it to XoshiroSIMD with SIMDRNG_DISPATCH=ON and to XoshiroNative (non-portable, build-host -march) by default, while docs/guides/xoshiro.rst says it falls back to XoshiroScalar. Name XoshiroScalar explicitly for per-call use.

Stream overlap when mixing types: XoshiroScalar(seed, t) jumps t times by 2^128, which is exactly lane t of XoshiroSIMD(seed); SIMD thread_id uses mid_jump (2^160) instead. Do not mix scalar thread streams and SIMD engines on the same seed.
On SIMD types jump(n) advances every lane by n (so n x SIMD_WIDTH outputs of the interleaved stream) and does not flush values already in the 256-entry cache (from xoshiro_simd.hpp).
Each SIMD instance carries a 2 KiB output cache plus up to 256 bytes of 64-byte-aligned state, and the runtime-dispatch types need the compiled library; they are not available from the single header.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick simdrng over Xoshiro256PlusSIMD or the xoshiro8x256pp gist when you want a maintained, tested package with runtime ISA dispatch, std-compatible engines, xoshiro256++ (not 256+) and Philox/ChaCha in one place. Pick VMT19937 instead if you must keep Mersenne Twister output, and SHISHUA or the AES-based testingRNG generators if raw byte throughput matters more than a standard algorithm.
verified_claims_summary: The project's CI Google Benchmark run (gcc-15, Release, -march=x86-64-v3, AMD EPYC 7763 GitHub runner, libstdc++) measured XoshiroSIMD bulk fill at 1645 ns per 4096 u64 vs 3835 ns for the scalar loop (about 2.3x), Philox4x32 3.5x and ChaCha20 2.8x SIMD over scalar fills. Against the standard library it measured per-call times only: std::mt19937_64 1.60 ns vs XoshiroScalar 0.94 ns, and std::mt19937_64 + std::uniform_real_distribution 8.01 ns vs XoshiroScalar::uniform() 1.32 ns; std::mt19937_64 was never timed in bulk.
status_note: Active (last commit 2026-07-22, 151 commits, CI on Linux/macOS/Windows with sanitizers and static analysis) but pre-1.0, single author, 3 stars, and under a BSD-3-Clause-Attribution license that requires an acknowledgement, so listed as reference rather than copyable.
